extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, news photo editors, documentary photographers, and readers interested in ethics and standards for image processing in news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for how news and documentary photographs may be processed or retouched while preserving journalistic integrity, including what adjustments are allowed, forbidden techniques, and expectations for transparency and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: No adding or removing content / material alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Material alteration to the image by including or excluding a certain item is not acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Narciso Contreras case (removing a colleague’s video camera) and stated explicitly by Reuters: "No additions or deletions to the subject matter of the original image (thus changing the original content and journalistic integrity of an image)." World Press Photo and other organizations reiterate that the content of images must not be altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain integrity of photographic content and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing should maintain the integrity of the photographic images’ content and context; do not manipulate images in any way that can mislead viewers or misrepresent subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the National Press Photographers Association code of ethics: "Editing should maintain the integrity of the photographic images’ content and context. Do not manipulate images or add or alter sound in any way that can mislead viewers or misrepresent subjects." Getty Images: images must be delivered with accuracy and impartiality, held to accountability equal to written journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and verifiability of processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals should make their work verifiable — document every processing step, provide a digital trail, and let readers see how an image was produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include making visible every Photoshop/Lightroom change, geotagging where the image was taken, who was involved, and providing metadata or a clickable icon that lists all processing applied to an online image. Quoted: "The more verifiable an image is, the more authentic it will be regarded as."

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'manipulation' vs 'processing' and use precise nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: "Manipulation" refers to moving actual pixels (with the exception of removing sensor dust), while "processing" is everything done to turn data into an image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise terms so audiences and editors can understand what was done; this distinction affects acceptability and verification expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor adjustments allowed when minimally necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor adjustments such as cropping, dodging and burning, conversion to grayscale, normal toning and color adjustments are acceptable if limited to those minimally necessary for clear and accurate reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP guidance: these adjustments should be analogous to darkroom burning and dodging and should restore the authentic nature of the photograph rather than alter it.

rubrics_metrics.name: No changes that substantially alter the original scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in density, contrast, color and saturation levels that substantially alter the original scene are not acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From AP: alterations that dramatically change the original lighting conditions or visual facts of the scene are disallowed. Reuters similarly warns against excessive lightening, darkening or blurring that misleads the viewer by disguising elements of an image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faces and identities must not be obscured by editing
rubrics_metrics.description: The faces or identities of individuals must not be obscured by Photoshop or any other editing tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct AP rule: preserving identification of people depicted is required; do not obscure identities via retouching or manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of red-eye is not permissible (per AP guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The removal of 'red eye' from photographs is not permissible according to the AP excerpt included in the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP lists this as an example of an impermissible edit in its stated rules; note that this is specific wording from AP's guidance as quoted in the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed technical operations and limits (Reuters example list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain technical adjustments are allowed if performed carefully and within limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reuters allowed list (as quoted): "Cropping, adjustment of Levels to histogram limits, minor colour correction, sharpening at 300%, 0.3, 0, careful use of lasso tool, subtle use of burn tool, adjustment of highlights and shadows, eye dropper to check/set gray." Treat these operations as permissible when used subtly and not to change factual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited tools and techniques (Reuters example list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific tools and techniques are explicitly disallowed because they can materially alter an image or mislead viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reuters not allowed list (as quoted): "Additions or deletions to image, cloning & Healing tool (except dust), airbrush, brush, paint, selective area sharpening, excessive lightening/darkening, excessive colour tone change, auto levels, blurring, eraser tool, quick mask, in-camera sharpening, in-camera saturation styles." Violation can lead to dismissal or removal of images from archives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retouching must conform to currently accepted industry standards (World Press Photo)
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the images must not be altered; only retouching which conforms to currently accepted standards in the industry is allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: World Press Photo submission guidance emphasizes adherence to prevailing, accepted standards for acceptable retouching when submitting to contests and publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical duty to avoid erosion of public trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Photojournalists have an ethical responsibility to avoid deceptive practices because manipulation erodes public trust and the ability of images to inform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple practitioners quoted (Stanley Greene, Fred Ritchin, Ron Haviv, Ashley Gilbertson) argue that maintaining trust and distinguishing nonfiction from fiction is central; the industry should prioritize verifiability and transparent practices to preserve credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/darkroom practices are not a definitive standard for digital edits
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptability should not simply be justified by what was done in the darkroom era because darkroom practice was itself varied and could include substantial alteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: David Campbell and others note that invoking darkroom practices as a benchmark is flawed—analog processes could be heavily manipulated, so digital acceptability requires clearer, contemporary standards and transparency rather than appeals to past practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for breaches of standards (archival removal, dismissal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material manipulation can lead to professional consequences such as severing ties, removal from public archives, and dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: AP removed Contreras's work from archives; Reuters notes material alteration will lead to dismissal. Organizations may rescind awards or remove images if standards are breached.
